CWE-20.name: Improper input validation
CWE-20.plain: The software trusts data it receives without checking it's the right type, size or format. Many other bug types start here.
CWE-20.defend: Check every input against what's allowed (type, length, format) and reject anything else.

CWE-22.name: Path traversal
CWE-22.plain: An attacker puts sequences like ../ in a file name to climb out of the folder they're meant to stay in, then reads or overwrites other files.
CWE-22.defend: Resolve the full path and confirm it's still inside the allowed folder before opening it.

CWE-74.name: Injection
CWE-74.plain: Attacker input is passed to another system (a database, shell or template) and gets treated as instructions instead of plain data.
CWE-74.defend: Keep data and commands separate: use parameterised APIs and encode output.

CWE-77.name: Command injection
CWE-77.plain: User input ends up inside a system command, so an attacker can add their own commands and run them on the server.
CWE-77.defend: Avoid the shell. Pass arguments as a list to safe APIs and allow-list expected values.

CWE-78.name: OS command injection
CWE-78.plain: User input ends up inside an operating-system command, so an attacker can tack on their own commands (e.g. ; rm -rf) and run them on the server.
CWE-78.defend: Avoid the shell. Pass arguments as a list to safe APIs and allow-list expected values.

CWE-79.name: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
CWE-79.plain: The site shows attacker-supplied text as live code in other people's browsers. The attacker can then act as those users: steal sessions, change settings, show fake login forms.
CWE-79.defend: Encode output for where it appears (HTML, attribute, JavaScript) and add a Content Security Policy.

CWE-89.name: SQL injection
CWE-89.plain: Input is pasted straight into a database query, so an attacker can rewrite the query to read, change or delete data they shouldn't touch.
CWE-89.defend: Use parameterised queries (prepared statements) every time. Never build SQL by joining strings.

CWE-94.name: Code injection
CWE-94.plain: The application runs attacker-controlled input as program code.
CWE-94.defend: Never eval() user input. Use safe parsers and run risky code in a sandbox.

CWE-119.name: Memory buffer error
CWE-119.plain: The program reads or writes outside the block of memory it was given. This can crash it, leak secrets, or let an attacker run their own code.
CWE-119.defend: Bounds-check every buffer, prefer memory-safe languages, keep mitigations like ASLR and DEP enabled.

CWE-120.name: Buffer overflow
CWE-120.plain: Data is copied into a fixed-size space without checking it fits, so it spills over and overwrites whatever is next in memory.
CWE-120.defend: Use length-checked copy functions and memory-safe languages.

CWE-121.name: Stack buffer overflow
CWE-121.plain: Too much data is written into a buffer on the stack, which can overwrite the return address and hijack the program's flow.
CWE-121.defend: Bounds checks, stack canaries and compiler hardening flags.

CWE-122.name: Heap buffer overflow
CWE-122.plain: Too much data is written into a buffer on the heap, corrupting nearby data structures that an attacker can then abuse.
CWE-122.defend: Bounds checks, hardened allocators and memory-safe languages.

CWE-125.name: Out-of-bounds read
CWE-125.plain: The program reads past the end of a block of memory. That can leak secrets (Heartbleed was one of these) or crash the program.
CWE-125.defend: Validate lengths and indexes before reading.

CWE-190.name: Integer overflow
CWE-190.plain: A number grows bigger than its type can hold and wraps around, like a car odometer rolling over to zero. The wrong number then leads to memory bugs.
CWE-190.defend: Check arithmetic before using the result for sizes or indexes.

CWE-200.name: Information exposure
CWE-200.plain: The software reveals information to someone who shouldn't see it, such as internal paths, user records or keys. Attackers use these leaks to plan the next step.
CWE-200.defend: Return generic errors, limit what APIs return, and review what's logged or exposed.

CWE-269.name: Improper privilege management
CWE-269.plain: The software hands out, keeps or fails to drop privileges properly, so a normal user can climb to admin.
CWE-269.defend: Least privilege: give each user and process only the access it needs.

CWE-276.name: Incorrect default permissions
CWE-276.plain: Files or settings are installed with permissions that let too many people read or change them.
CWE-276.defend: Ship locked-down defaults and audit permissions after install.

CWE-284.name: Improper access control
CWE-284.plain: The rules about who can do what are missing or broken.
CWE-284.defend: Enforce access checks on the server for every request.

CWE-287.name: Improper authentication
CWE-287.plain: The software doesn't properly prove you are who you say you are, so an attacker can log in as someone else.
CWE-287.defend: Use well-tested login frameworks, MFA and secure session handling.

CWE-295.name: Improper certificate validation
CWE-295.plain: The software doesn't properly check HTTPS certificates, so someone in the middle of the connection can pretend to be the real server.
CWE-295.defend: Use the platform's default TLS validation and never disable it in production.

CWE-306.name: Missing authentication
CWE-306.plain: An important function works with no login at all. Anyone who can reach it can use it.
CWE-306.defend: Require authentication on every sensitive function, including admin and API endpoints.

CWE-312.name: Cleartext storage of sensitive data
CWE-312.plain: Passwords, keys or personal data are stored unencrypted, so anyone who gets the file or database can read them.
CWE-312.defend: Encrypt sensitive data at rest and hash passwords with a slow algorithm like bcrypt or Argon2.

CWE-327.name: Broken or risky cryptography
CWE-327.plain: The software uses an outdated or weak encryption method that attackers know how to break.
CWE-327.defend: Use modern, well-reviewed libraries and algorithms (AES-GCM, SHA-256 or better).

CWE-347.name: Improper signature verification
CWE-347.plain: The software doesn't properly check digital signatures, so tampered files or tokens are accepted as genuine.
CWE-347.defend: Always verify signatures with a trusted library and reject anything unsigned.

CWE-352.name: Cross-site request forgery (CSRF)
CWE-352.plain: A malicious website makes your browser send a request to another site where you're already logged in, like changing your email or password, without you knowing.
CWE-352.defend: Use anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies.

CWE-362.name: Race condition
CWE-362.plain: Two things happen at almost the same time and the software doesn't handle the overlap, letting an attacker slip in between a check and an action.
CWE-362.defend: Use proper locking and make check-and-act steps atomic.

CWE-400.name: Uncontrolled resource consumption
CWE-400.plain: An attacker can make the software use up memory, CPU or disk until it slows down or falls over. This is a denial-of-service bug.
CWE-400.defend: Set limits, timeouts and rate limiting on expensive operations.

CWE-416.name: Use after free
CWE-416.plain: The program keeps using a piece of memory after it has given it back. If an attacker fills that spot with their own data, they can often take control.
CWE-416.defend: Clear pointers after freeing, use smart pointers or memory-safe languages.

CWE-427.name: Uncontrolled search path
CWE-427.plain: The program looks for libraries or files in folders an attacker can write to, so it loads the attacker's planted file instead (DLL hijacking).
CWE-427.defend: Load from absolute, trusted paths only.

CWE-434.name: Unrestricted file upload
CWE-434.plain: The site accepts uploaded files without checking what they are, so an attacker can upload a script (a web shell) and run it on the server.
CWE-434.defend: Allow-list file types, rename uploads, and store them where they can't be executed.

CWE-476.name: NULL pointer dereference
CWE-476.plain: The program tries to use something that doesn't exist and crashes. Usually a denial-of-service bug.
CWE-476.defend: Check for null before use; memory-safe languages prevent most of these.

CWE-502.name: Deserialisation of untrusted data
CWE-502.plain: The app rebuilds objects from data it received. Crafted data can make it run attacker code while rebuilding them.
CWE-502.defend: Never deserialise untrusted data with native formats; use simple formats like JSON with strict schemas.

CWE-522.name: Weakly protected credentials
CWE-522.plain: Passwords or keys are stored or sent in a way that's easy to steal.
CWE-522.defend: Hash passwords properly, encrypt secrets, and send them only over TLS.

CWE-532.name: Sensitive data in log files
CWE-532.plain: Passwords, tokens or personal data get written into logs, where far more people and systems can read them.
CWE-532.defend: Scrub secrets before logging and restrict who can read logs.

CWE-601.name: Open redirect
CWE-601.plain: A link on a trusted site can be made to forward visitors anywhere. Phishers use it so their links look legitimate.

CWE-639.name: Insecure direct object reference (IDOR)
CWE-639.plain: Changing an ID in a request (like /invoice/1001 to /invoice/1002) shows someone else's data because the app never checks who owns it.
CWE-639.defend: Check ownership on the server for every object a user requests.

CWE-732.name: Incorrect permission assignment
CWE-732.plain: A critical file, folder or resource can be changed by users who shouldn't have that power.
CWE-732.defend: Apply least privilege to files and services and audit them regularly.

CWE-770.name: No limits on resource allocation
CWE-770.plain: The software lets a request reserve as much memory or as many connections as it asks for, so an attacker can exhaust them.
CWE-770.defend: Cap sizes, counts and time per request.

CWE-787.name: Out-of-bounds write
CWE-787.plain: The program writes past the end of a block of memory, corrupting nearby data. Skilled attackers turn this into running their own code. It's #1 on MITRE's most dangerous list.
CWE-787.defend: Bounds-check writes, prefer memory-safe languages, keep exploit mitigations on.

CWE-798.name: Hard-coded credentials
CWE-798.plain: A password or key is baked into the software itself. Anyone who finds it can log in to every device running that version.
CWE-798.defend: Never ship built-in passwords; force unique credentials on setup.

CWE-862.name: Missing authorisation
CWE-862.plain: The app checks that you're logged in, but not whether you're allowed to do this particular thing.
CWE-862.defend: Check permissions on the server for every action, not just login.

CWE-863.name: Incorrect authorisation
CWE-863.plain: A permission check exists but gets it wrong, so some users can do things they shouldn't.
CWE-863.defend: Centralise permission checks and test them with different user roles.

CWE-917.name: Expression language injection
CWE-917.plain: Input is evaluated by a template or expression engine, letting attackers run code. This was the root cause of Log4Shell.
CWE-917.defend: Never evaluate user input as an expression; disable lookups you don't need.

CWE-918.name: Server-side request forgery (SSRF)
CWE-918.plain: The attacker makes the server send web requests for them, often to internal systems or cloud metadata services that aren't reachable from outside.
CWE-918.defend: Allow-list destinations and block internal IP ranges from server-side fetches.

CWE-1321.name: Prototype pollution
CWE-1321.plain: In JavaScript, attacker input changes the base object that all other objects inherit from, which can change app behaviour or lead to code execution.
CWE-1321.defend: Freeze prototypes, validate keys like __proto__, and use Map for user-keyed data.

CWE-1333.name: Inefficient regular expression (ReDoS)
CWE-1333.plain: A badly written pattern can take forever on a crafted input, freezing the app.
CWE-1333.defend: Use linear-time regex engines or limit input length and matching time.
